# Running Harley for 100 miles with no oil

The scenario described in the source material presents a catastrophic failure mode common to internal combustion engines: operating without lubrication. The bike had an oil change performed, yet the crankcase remained empty. Despite this, the rider managed 124 miles before hearing loud noises and pulling over. Upon inspection, the motor was real hot. This specific sequence of events highlights a critical misunderstanding of engine physics that often leads to total loss of the asset.

When an internal combustion engine starts without oil, hydrodynamic lubrication does not exist immediately. The crankshaft bearings, camshafts, and piston walls rely on a thin film of oil to separate metal surfaces. Without this fluid, the coefficient of friction spikes instantly from 0.1 to over 2.0. The heat generated is exponential because friction converts kinetic energy directly into thermal energy rather than mechanical work. The rider likely experienced "metal-on-metal" seizure risks during those first few hundred miles, which explains why the engine started making loud noises after the initial run.

The decision made by the service shop to add diesel oil instead of SAE 20W-50 or similar motorcycle-specific lubricant was a significant technical error. Diesel oil is formulated for compression ratios and combustion characteristics found in diesel engines, not high-revving V-twin motorcycles. More importantly, diesel oils often lack the extreme pressure (EP) additives required to protect valve train components under high load. Furthermore, mixing diesel fuel into the crankcase can alter the viscosity of any residual fluids or introduce contaminants that clog oil passages designed for thinner motor oil.

The immediate drop in power ("half power") upon adding the wrong oil confirms that the engine was already damaged. The pistons likely scored the cylinder walls during the initial 124-mile run, creating a rough surface that prevents proper sealing. This reduces compression, leading to poor combustion and loss of torque. The subsequent appearance of smoke indicates severe overheating. When an engine runs without oil, the heat soak causes the piston crowns and cylinder heads to expand beyond their design limits. This can warp the head gasket or even crack the block itself.

The fact that the engine now only spins when cranked suggests a mechanical seizure. The connecting rod bearings have almost certainly failed completely, causing the rod to bend or break free from the crankshaft journal. Alternatively, the camshaft lobes may have worn down to the point where they can no longer lift the valves, or the pistons are fused to the cylinder walls due to thermal expansion and carbon buildup. In either case, the engine block has suffered irreversible damage.

Attempting to ride a motorcycle after an oil starvation event is akin to running production code without memory management. The system might appear to function initially, but the underlying architecture is compromised. The heat generated during the first 124 miles likely softened the piston rings or melted the anti-seize compound on the spark plugs. Adding diesel oil did not repair the damage; it merely masked the symptoms long enough for further destruction to occur.

The only viable path forward is a complete engine rebuild or replacement of the cylinder kit and bearings. Replacing just the oil will not restore the engine's integrity because the physical geometry of the internal components has been altered by heat and friction. The cost of repairing the bike will likely exceed its market value, making scrapping the unit the rational economic decision.

For developers managing hardware systems or IoT devices with embedded engines, this case study serves as a reminder that resource allocation is non-negotiable. Just as a microcontroller cannot execute instructions without power, an internal combustion engine cannot operate without lubrication. The margin for error in such systems is zero.
